title: LC4 and LPLC2 retinotopic synaptic gradients onto escape neurons repeat in four hemispheres of two fly connectomes, and gradient directions of 418 VPN-target units agree between animals
abstract: Question: Dombrovski et al. (2023) found that LC4 neurons that look to the front put more synapses onto the escape descending neuron DNp02, and neurons that look to the back put more onto DNp11, from 55 hand-traced neurons in one FAFB hemisphere. Do such retinotopic output gradients repeat in other animals, and are the gradients of all visual projection neuron (VPN) types a fixed wiring rule? Approach: we used four complete hemispheres of FlyWire FAFB v783 (female) and the male CNS v1.0 (male). Each VPN neuron received an eye position from the column positions of its columnar inputs; the A-P and D-V axes came from anatomy only. For each VPN type, target type and side, a Poisson model with an output offset gave the gradient, tested with 2,000 permutations; tests were set before fitting. Results: LC4 to DNp02 increased to the front (1.18 to 1.47 times per SD), LC4 to DNp11 decreased (0.55 to 0.61), and LPLC2 to the giant fiber increased to the top (1.32 to 1.48), with p at most 0.001 in all four hemispheres. In 32 to 33 VPN types, 76% to 81% of 604 to 861 target units per hemisphere had a position effect (FDR 5%). For 418 units in all hemispheres, gradients agreed between animals with r 0.96 to 0.97 (A-P) and 0.94 to 0.95 (D-V), nearly as well as between the two hemispheres of one animal (0.98, 0.96); a within-type target shuffle gave r 0.02 to 0.08. Native axes and removal of eye-edge neurons did not change the results. Limitations: two animals of different sex and method; FlyWire is the same animal as the original study; structural replication only, with no activity or behaviour data. Code, unit-level results, figures and data hashes are included; per-neuron extracts are regenerated from CC BY 4.0 sources.
